title: Wood that turned to stone
teaches: Why most living things leave no trace, and the chemistry that turns wood, shell and soft bodies into fossils

blocks.text: In the Painted Desert of northeastern Arizona, in what is now Petrified Forest National Park, hundreds of fallen tree trunks lie on the ground in pieces. Many are broken into short sections with clean, square ends, as if someone had cut them for firewood. Pick one up and it is far too heavy for wood: it is stone, mostly quartz, banded in red, yellow and purple. Yet the outside still shows bark, and a polished end shows the growth rings, and under a microscope the walls of the individual cells, each a few hundredths of a millimetre across.

blocks.caption: Petrified logs in Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona. The trees grew about 220 million years ago.

blocks.text: The trees were conifers that grew about 220 million years ago, when this part of Arizona lay close to the equator in the supercontinent of Pangaea (lesson 8). How did wood become stone and keep detail too fine to see with the naked eye? And why are fossils like this rare, when trees have been falling for hundreds of millions of years?

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The logs at Petrified Forest are quartz, yet they keep bark, growth rings and individual cells.
They are about 220 million years old.

blocks.text: Almost everything that dies is destroyed. Scavengers eat it; **decomposers**, the fungi and bacteria that feed on dead tissue, digest the rest. Most decomposers need oxygen, and the fastest of them, such as the fungi that break down lignin (the tough material that stiffens wood), cannot work without it. A log lying on a forest floor is gone in a few decades to a century or two. Even bone and shell, which are largely mineral, are broken up by trampling, waves and rain, and slowly dissolved by slightly acidic water.

The first condition for a fossil is to escape all that by being buried quickly, in sediment that keeps oxygen out. Fine mud on a still lake or sea floor does this well; so does volcanic ash, or sand dumped by a flood. The second condition is chemistry: what the water soaking through the sediment is carrying, and what it does to the buried remains over thousands to millions of years. How quickly and how completely the oxygen is shut out decides whether anything soft survives long enough for that chemistry to act; the chemistry decides what it becomes.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Scavengers and decomposers destroy most remains; decomposers work fastest with oxygen.
A fossil first needs quick burial away from oxygen.
What the groundwater carries then decides what kind of fossil forms.

parts.title: Filling the spaces, then replacing the walls

blocks.text: Wood is a honeycomb. Each cell is a long, hollow tube with a wall of cellulose and lignin around an empty space, and much of a log's volume is that empty space, filled with air or water. When a buried log is soaked in groundwater carrying dissolved minerals, those minerals can crystallise out of the water inside the empty spaces, in the same way that limescale (calcium carbonate) builds up inside a kettle. For wood, the commonest such mineral is silica (silicon dioxide, the substance of quartz). Over time it fills every cell space, while the walls are still the original wood. This is **permineralization**: the minerals are added, the original material remains.

Over a longer time, the wood of the walls itself can go. Even without oxygen, water very slowly breaks down cellulose and lignin chemically, and as each tiny piece of a wall dissolves, silica crystallises in its place. Because the wall is rebuilt a few molecules at a time, far smaller than the wall itself, its shape survives, now built of quartz. This is **replacement**. Petrified wood is usually a mixture of both: in a thin slice under a microscope, some of the walls are still dark remains of the original wood, and others are silica throughout.

blocks.caption: A slice across buried wood, cells enlarged. Silica comes out of the groundwater first in the empty cell spaces, then replaces the walls. The rates are illustrative: real petrification ranges from centuries in hot springs to millions of years.
blocks.task: Turn the walls themselves to quartz

blocks.text: Where does the silica come from? At Petrified Forest the logs were carried by rivers and buried in sand and mud that included large amounts of volcanic ash, blown from volcanoes to the southwest. Volcanic ash is glass, chilled so fast it never crystallised (lesson 4), and glass dissolves much more readily than crystals, releasing silica into the groundwater. The water percolating through the ash was rich in silica, and the buried logs soaked it up. Traces of iron and manganese came with it and gave the stone its reds, yellows and purples.

blocks.caption: A polished slice of petrified wood. The growth rings and the outline of the bark survive in quartz.

blocks.text: The neat breaks came much later. Quartz is brittle. As the rock layers holding the logs were lifted and flexed, and as erosion exposed them, the long stone trunks cracked across at intervals, the way a long glass rod snaps cleanly instead of bending.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Permineralization: minerals fill the empty spaces, while the original walls remain.
Replacement: the original material dissolves piece by piece and minerals take its place, keeping its shape.
Volcanic ash dissolves easily and supplies the silica that petrifies wood.

blocks.text: Silica is one of several routes, and the conditions of burial pick the route.

**Carbon films.** If the remains are flattened under more and more sediment without much mineral-rich water, heat and pressure drive off their hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen as water, carbon dioxide and methane. What is left is a thin black film of carbon in the shape of the original, a leaf, a fern frond, a fish. This is a **compression** fossil. Coal is the same process applied to a whole swamp of plants. The soft-bodied animals of the Burgess Shale in British Columbia, about 508 million years old, are preserved as films like this, with the outlines of guts and legs.

blocks.caption: A fossil fern preserved as a film of carbon on a split rock surface.

blocks.text: **Pyrite.** On a sea floor with no oxygen, a different set of bacteria takes over. Seawater carries dissolved sulphate, and these bacteria use it in place of oxygen to digest dead tissue, releasing hydrogen sulphide (the smell of rotten eggs). The sulphide meets dissolved iron in the mud and forms iron sulphide, eventually **pyrite**, the brassy mineral called fool's gold. If it forms right around the decaying body, it can copy the soft parts in metal-coloured mineral. In 1892 a fossil collector named William Valiant found a thin layer of shale near Rome, New York, in which the trilobites (extinct sea creatures with jointed shells) keep their legs and antennae in pyrite. Charles Beecher of Yale studied them, and the layer is now called Beecher's Trilobite Bed.

blocks.caption: A trilobite, Triarthrus eatoni, from Beecher's Trilobite Bed in New York. Its legs and antennae are preserved in pyrite.

blocks.text: **Moulds and casts.** A shell made of calcite or aragonite (forms of calcium carbonate) can survive burial for a long time, but groundwater that is slightly acidic, as rainwater carrying carbon dioxide often is, dissolves it. The shell disappears, leaving a hollow in the rock in its shape, a **mould**. If minerals later fill the hollow, they make a **cast**, a copy of the shell's shape in different material. Where the water instead carries plenty of dissolved lime, it does not dissolve the shell, which may survive almost unchanged. Other hard parts can last the same way: Steno's tongue stones in lesson 1, fossil shark teeth, were still their original tooth mineral.

blocks.caption: A log, a shell and a soft-bodied worm are buried. Choose how fast, whether the bottom water has oxygen, and what the groundwater carries. The rules are a simplification: in nature these routes overlap.
blocks.task: Find the conditions that turn the log to quartz

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Compression leaves a carbon film when heat and pressure drive off everything but carbon.
Without oxygen, bacteria turn seawater sulphate to sulphide, which forms pyrite with iron, sometimes copying soft parts.
Dissolved shells leave moulds; minerals filling the moulds make casts.

blocks.text: Because each route needs particular conditions, the fossil record is a biased sample of past life. Hard parts, shells, bones and teeth, are far more likely to survive than soft ones. Animals that lived where sediment was settling, on sea floors and lake beds and river plains, are more likely to be buried than those living on hillsides or mountains, where erosion wins. A place like the Burgess Shale or Beecher's bed, where soft bodies such as worms and jellyfish could be preserved, is a rare window, and geologists treat such sites, called **Lagerstätten** (German for storage places), as precious for exactly that reason.

This bias matters for lesson 3. William Smith identified layers by the fossils in them, and those fossils were mostly shells: common, hard, and living on sea floors where sediment fell. The fossils that told him which layer he stood on were the ones both burial and chemistry favour.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The fossil record favours hard parts and animals that lived where sediment was settling.
Sites that preserve soft bodies (Lagerstätten) are rare and especially valuable.

blocks.caption: Six questions on how fossils form
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why does quick burial in fine mud help a body become a fossil?
choices: It keeps out oxygen and scavengers, so decay slows
Mud is warm enough to bake the body hard
Mud contains the silica that replaces wood
items.why: Scavengers and most decomposers need access and oxygen. Mud sealing the body off gives chemistry time to act before the remains are destroyed.

items.ask: What is the difference between permineralization and replacement?
choices: Permineralization fills the empty spaces while the original material remains; replacement swaps the original material itself for minerals
Permineralization happens on land, replacement in the sea
Replacement only affects bones, permineralization only wood
items.why: In permineralization minerals are added in the pores. In replacement the original material dissolves piece by piece and minerals take its place, keeping its shape.

items.ask: Why did volcanic ash help petrify the Arizona logs?
choices: Ash is glass, which dissolves easily and fills groundwater with silica
Hot ash baked the wood into stone
Ash kept the logs frozen until they were buried
items.why: Glass dissolves far more readily than crystalline rock. Water soaking through the ash carried silica into the buried wood.

items.ask: How does pyrite form around a body on a sea floor with no oxygen?
choices: Bacteria use seawater sulphate to digest the tissue, and the sulphide they release combines with iron
Iron in the blood crystallises as the body dries
Volcanic gases deposit iron sulphide on the sea floor
items.why: Sulphate-reducing bacteria produce hydrogen sulphide, which reacts with dissolved iron in the mud to make iron sulphide and eventually pyrite.

items.ask: How was this fossil fern preserved?
choices: As a carbon film: pressure and heat drove off most of the other elements, leaving carbon
As pyrite, in mud without oxygen
As a mould, after the plant dissolved
items.why: Compression drives off hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, leaving a thin dark film of carbon in the shape of the leaf.

items.ask: Why are fossils of shells far more common than fossils of jellyfish?
choices: Hard parts resist decay and survive burial far more often than soft tissue
Jellyfish have always lived only in fresh water, where no sediment settles
Shellfish lived in greater numbers than any soft-bodied animal
items.why: Soft tissue needs rare conditions to be preserved. Shells are mineral already and can survive ordinary burial.

learned: Fossils need quick burial away from oxygen, then the right groundwater chemistry.
Permineralization fills pores with minerals; replacement swaps the original material for minerals while keeping its shape.
Carbon films, pyrite, moulds and casts are other routes, each set by the conditions of burial.
The fossil record favours hard parts and places where sediment was settling.
